utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Case, IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Registrar, and good morning to you. And Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours and good morning to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben lead counsel for the Prosecution, and I'm here together with my co-counsel Ms. Joanne Richardson and our case manager is Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, my learned friends, my name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant Ms. Adisa Mehic and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, two issues. First issue is the witness schedule according to the latest notifications by the Prosecution. With respect to the witnesses we would like to file today to circulate among parties a new witness schedule. We hope to do that by -- after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Second issue is related to a chain of custody witness and I requested Ms. Joanne Richardson to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank, Your Honour. Good morning. Your Honour, this matter is with respect to the recalling of the witness Nikola Popovic. I think the matter was raised earlier this week and I don't know if the Chamber and the Defence have had an opportunity to review the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have reviewed the transcript. There is no such reservation. However, to cut it short, if you are not planning to bring this witness over, I still cannot pre-empt the issue of having him recalled, should there be an ad hoc application motion by the Defence and they of course would have to show cause why he should be recalled. In other words, we would have -- we would require a -- very clearly spelled out, the questions that they need to put to him and why they couldn't be put earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's the position. I mean we're -- I don't think we need --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I thank you for that because that would have been part of my submission this morning that in fact that the Defence be required to spell out exactly what areas they'd like to raise that they were not able to the last time he was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I would just like to advise the Court with respect to the logbook that was turned over to our investigator that the logbook was examined by the Defence. It is for all intents and purposes the exact copy of the exact -- of the copy that was used here by Mr. Popovic and was given over and that was promised to be turned over to the investigator. There is, I believe, one additional element to the original and that is there is a calendar page, but for all intents and purposes, it is the exact same as the original and so with that said, I think the Defence would certainly have to show good cause why they are seeking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't -- we don't have an application as yet. So let's wait for the application and then we see and we talk about it because you're trying to pre-empt the issue. You're also making a statement instead of a submission or you're presenting the facts that -- what has the original is exactly the same as the copy provided earlier. This should be made as a submission and not as a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour I'll wait for the Defence to make it that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic might as well stand up and say exactly the opposite. How do I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour, and if the Defence is not prepared today to make a submission that's all I'll say on that matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I mean, I don't expect you to stand up and respond to this. If you file -- if you need this Mr. Popovic back here, to have him recalled, as I understand he's not going to be brought forward by the Prosecution, then you need to file an ad hoc application or motion, whatever you call it, and we will consider it on its own merit. All right. Thank you. Yes. Can we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Okanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should be receiving interpretation of what I am saying in English into your own language. It's important for me to have a confirmation of this. If at any time there are problems with interpretation, please let us know. I am the Presiding Judge in this trial against Naser Oric, my name is Carmel Agius, and I come from Malta. To my right I have Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark. To my left I have Judge Albin Eser from Germany. Together we form the Trial Chamber in this case. You are here to give evidence as a witness of the Prosecution and our Rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration, something which is equivalent to an oath in some jurisdictions, to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration is contained on a piece of paper that Madam Usher is going to hand to you now. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Okanovic. You may sit down. You are planned to testify over two days, today and then Monday, when you are supposed to finish. Much depends on how brief and how precise your answers will be. My suggestion to you is that you try to answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question and not to give us information that is not being asked of you in the questions that are put to you. You will be asked a number of questions by Ms. Richardson and when the -- what we call the examination-in-chief is finished, she will then be followed by Mr. Jones, who is appearing for Naser Oric. So Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Richardson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Okanovic. Please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Milos Okanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please confirm the following information, if I may lead just briefly, Your Honour. You were born on the 19th of November 1949 and you are of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You presently reside in Serbia in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vhrpolje. That is a hamlet of Grabovica to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your village or your hamlet is located across the Drina River from Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You resided in this hamlet of Grabovica in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a -- an electrical engineer by profession and you have been doing this since 1976?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are presently employed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are also a radio amateur?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was. I don't have time for it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You completed your compulsory military service in 1976?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were not mobilised during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask Mr. Okanovic about your knowledge of the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac. Prior to 1992 had you visited these areas?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: From 1979 until 1983 I lived in Bratunac and worked in the tile factory called Kaolin. I resided in Bratunac at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you ever visited Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Often, often in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a point in 1992, and I'll refer you specifically to the -- early 1992, that you were aware that a conflict had erupted in and around the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Even before that, there were tensions and of course I learned about all this, there was shooting on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where, if you could, tell us where the shooting, what areas the shooting occurred in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: From the area across the Drina. I lived near the Drina and you could often hear shooting from that side, both nearby and far away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, let's be a little bit -- I know that in your previous question you had referred the witness to early in 1992 but let's be a little bit more specific as to when this shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or when he started noticing these shootings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic you heard His Honour's question. Could you tell us exactly when it was in 1992 you first began hearing shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't even say whether it was in 1992 or 1991. I can't speak about the date now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was there anything in particular that may have occurred in 1992 that made you aware that there was conflict in the Srebrenica area? Other than the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Allow me to interrupt you. When did the war start, Mr. Okanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period, but when precisely, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did you hear the shooting before the war started or after the war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the war started, that's when the shooting started. There was no shooting before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we've more or less fixed the date, Ms. Richardson. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to bring your attention to December of 1992. Do you recall that particular month?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And specifically December 14th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to December of 1992, I'd just like to take you back briefly to the village of Bjelovac. Do you recall what the ethnic makeup of the village was prior to December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed village before, before the beginning of the war. There were both Serbs and Muslims living there. utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In December of 1992, do you know if there were -- if the village was still mixed? In other words, were there still Serbs and Muslims living there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume not. I don't know because I wasn't there, but the war had already broken out and they separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, which ethnic resided in the village of Bjelovac in and around December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On December 14th, 1992, do you recall anything of significance happening in the village of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what time you first became aware that something was happening in the village?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the daily shooting, which didn't mean anything special, houses were set on fire and you could see the smoke rising from the hamlet of Sikiric, I think that's what it was called, in Bjelovac, the shooting was somewhat more intensive, which meant that some sort of operations were underway. Later on, you could see planes -- well, that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just go back just a bit. What were you able to see from your village in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was able to see only burning houses. I couldn't see who was setting fire to them or how. I could only see that the houses were burning. I didn't see the flames because the houses were built of brick, so the flames remained inside, but you could see the smoke billowing out and later on, at about 9.00, I was able to see the planes circling above and firing and also being fired at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were the houses burning before the planes arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: About half an hour or an hour before that, I went out of my house and saw that. That was before I took my camera. It was about an hour later. But the houses were already burning when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated -- you also testified that you heard shooting. Could you tell in what direction the shooting was coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell -- it was the shootings actually occurring in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell who was doing the shooting? Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you began to videotape the events that you were observing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly when you started videotaping and where you were when you began videotaping?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be precise but it was around 9.00. I can't be precise about the time. On the videotape, I put the date and the time, and you can see that on the videotape. You asked me something else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll ask you one thing at a time. Where were you when you were filming?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. I was on the roof of a low building when I was videotaping this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you able to --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: And that building is in my yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you able to videotape?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: What I could see with the naked eye, the smoke billowing from the houses, and you can hear the shooting and the planes participating in the fighting, obviously participating in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people around as you were filming the events that were occurring in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some villagers around me but I don't know exactly who or how many because I don't remember anymore. A lot of time has elapsed since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time if I could have a moment to be sure that we are ready to show the tape? Okay. At this time we had like to show the videotape to the witness and to have him narrate for us as we are looking at the film. Your Honour we do have transcripts of the videotape to hand out and this is Prosecution's Exhibit 316.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if there is a B/C/S version. That would assist, obviously, ourselves and our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a B/C/S version, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No we don't have the transcript in B/C/S but they are speaking in B/C/S. But we can provide this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think he should be in a position to hear the --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's really for us just to verify as we go along that it's correct. Yes, we'll verify the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it is a draft translation, Your Honour, and as we are reading the translation it may be the case that the witness may be able to even give us some additional information that's not here. So we'll see as we are reading along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps one other thing that could be done is the interpreters who will be also hearing the original sound track could translate as we go along without looking at this, in other words, if it is at all possible, so that in the meantime we can, while we listen to what you have to say, check whether there is any particular variance with the draft translation that we have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that very much depends on the sound quality. Usually the sound quality is far too poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's too poor then obviously that can't be done. But let's be positive about it and see how it works out. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour for the record the video starts at 26.08.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: 084. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic - can you just pause for a moment - can you just tell us what we've just seen? What are we looking at in the video?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a fraction of the neighbouring house. That's all I could see. Plus the date and the time that this was taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the video that you filmed on December 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the question was put while the video was freezed at 26.223. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sound you can hear is the sound of the plane. And in the background, you can see smoke rising from houses over near Bjelovac or Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the record, the statement that the witness has just made was made while the video was freezed at 26.315.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Sikiric. I can tell now with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the statement made by the witness is when the video is freezed at 26.495.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the plane that was involved in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness made this statement while the video was freezed at 27.458.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sound you can hear is someone firing at the plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, this statement was made by the witness while the video was freezed at 27.587.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic could you tell -- I'll repeat the question. Could you tell what type of plane that is that we are seeing on the video?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is a plane normally used for agricultural purposes. I'm not sure about the type. It's a very small plane, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, the witness's answer to the type of plane is 28.225?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, we just saw something fly across the screen. Could you tell us -- could we go back just a bit?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We just saw something fly across the screen on the videotape. Could you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were pigeons. If you rewind the tape slightly, I wasn't looking closely but I think those were pigeons. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness is referring to the still that occurs at 29.018.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are pigeons, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we see pigeons flying through again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, we see the plane flying over an area. Could you tell us what area the plane is flying over?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's flying over Bjelovac. It must have been crossing into Serbia because the whole area is very small. The way I see it now, it's probably flying right over my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, for the record, the statement made by the witness at 30.118.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm taping the plane from below, which would put it roughly over our heads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, this occurs at 30.194. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you can hear now, the conversation, this is someone next to me using a ham radio, a hand-held radio. I'm not sure who the speaker is but this is radio communication. That's the voices you can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement is made at 31.321.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is -- someone standing next to me is talking. This is no longer radio communication. It's just someone standing next to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This statement was made by the witness at 32.423.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are commenting on the way the plane is going around and what the plane is doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This statement is made for the record at 32.581.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, this statement is made at 33.213.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, again, the person standing next to me is saying that there is a house on fire, so there must be smoke coming out from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement by the witness is made at 33.486.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is obviously a young boy there addressing me as uncle and asking me, "Miko is the one flying the plane," but I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record this statement is made by the witness at 34.152.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can stop the tape, please. You can also hear a cock crow and hens or chickens. Somebody's cock. So the timing on this video must be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, this statement is made by the witness at 34.378.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, this young boy is asking me who is firing? And I'm replying, well, it's not our men because our men weren't shooting. That's what I told him. And when I said, "Our men," the implication was Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record this statement is made by the witness at 34.561.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we are commenting what's happening to our men, have very been surrounded, have they been cut off simply because we can't see anybody. All you can see is the general view. You can see the houses but there are no men around to be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement is made by the witness at 35.155.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person is saying, let's go and give them a hand. That's what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement is made by the witness at 35.289.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that I didn't see myself. There is someone shouting somewhere for me to try to tape some people carrying something, carrying sacks, apparently, but this is not something I saw at the time, nor was it something that I could tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement is made by the witness at 36.121. Yes. You can ask the question yourself, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: The voices which we heard have these voices come from people around you or from somewhere else? The last voices which we had heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person must be standing quite close to me because the voice is clear but there is another person shouting that wasn't so clear. So this other person may have been 20 or 30 metres away from where we were standing and he was probably in a position to see something else happening but from where I was standing there was no way that I could see it happening, what he said was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser, and thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something else here. There was quite a crowd there. Some people were near the road and some had climbed on to the roofs to watch, and you can hear a great many voices. It's difficult to make out who was saying what. I tried to focus on the taping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record this statement is made by the witness at 36.289.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can hear people commenting over the radio that's next to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record this statement is made by the witness at 37.199.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these comments are made over the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement is made by the witness at 37.536.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is someone commenting over the radio and there is a reference to a bird here but the person probably means just a plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record this statement is made by the witness at 38.279. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, the houses that we see in front of us that's on the screen at the moment, where are those houses? Is that in your village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's be more specific. In the foreground, in the foreground, not in the background. In the foreground. This is what you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These houses are all in my immediate neighbourhood. In the background, you can see the Drina River, which is the border line, and right behind it, you can see houses burning. That means is that this whole field, you can see here, belongs to Serbia and across the river, you find Bosnia and Bjelovac more specifically, I think, the hamlet of Sikiric. The centre of Bjelovac is further down to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Witness, and that has been most helpful. For the record we were still at 38.279 when the witness was explaining this. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can play the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these houses you can see here are in Serbia. That's my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This statement is made by the witness at 39.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, the voices we just heard, can you tell us if those are voices of people around you or is this also voices that you're picking up on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is radio communication. This is a conversation occurring over the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a call sign from Kojak to someone referred to as red or green. I'm not sure. This is a textbook example of radio communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the question was put and answered at 39.368.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This comment being made is being made by someone who is standing next to me. This person is counting the bombs that were dropped by the plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This statement is made at 39.465.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, the last one was 39.495 rather than 465. I thought I just correct that for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was reversed a bit and that is what I consider to be the still is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine. I was looking at it at the time, and it was to help, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not going to make a difference, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This sound right now, a tractor was probably driving by down the village road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This statement is made by the witness at 40.386.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're saying now that the plane hit something. That's someone next to me commenting on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record this statement is made by the witness at 42.164. Judge Eser, do you want to put your question? It's okay. Thank you. I think we better put it actually. En passant during the last minute or so we did again see across the screen things flying. Those I assume are still pigeons or birds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were a lot of pigeons there. I forgot to show you a lot of birds, a lot of pigeons on the roof. So everything that flies by quickly, that's them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are my neighbours standing around me and commenting on what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This statement is made by the witness at 43.028. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another thing. They are talking about someone but I really didn't see anyone. They are talking as if they can see somebody. I tried but I couldn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness makes this statement at 43.249.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This first part that you see here is the fields in Serbia, and behind the trees is the River Drina, and behind that is Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness makes this statement at 43.520.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These houses you can see here now, they are in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness makes this statement at 42.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, it's 44, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 44, yes, thank you. Thank you, Ms. Richardson. 44.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm standing on the bank of the Drina now. I've arrived at the river bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record the witness makes this statement at 44.300.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid being seen, I was behind the trees. There are lots of trees along the river bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement is made by the witness at 44.472.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you can hear shooting, that's probably some kind of fighting going on and everything you see now is in Bosnia. This is the hamlet of Sikiric, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record the witness makes this statement at 45.452.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another comment by your leave. I am very close to it now, but even now I didn't manage to see anyone. I didn't see any soldiers or anyone. There was shooting but you couldn't see anyone. They were probably all very well concealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness makes this statement at 46.172.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, this is another type of plane, obviously, with two wings, and it threw something out, a bomb or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness makes this statement at 47.564. Yes, Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: In the meantime, quite a bit of time elapsed. Had -- when you took the last sequence of the video, have you been still down at the Drina River or had you come back to your house? And where did the voices come from which we heard in this last part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In this last part, I've returned home, and I was taping from my home. I spent a short time on the river bank. I don't know whether somebody shot at me on purpose or whether it was by accident, but I felt a bullet whiz past and then I withdrew. Although I didn't see anyone on the other side. So I was on the bank of the Drina for a very short period of time. And, of course, it wasn't normal for me to be there because there was a lot of shooting, and it was nearby so you could get hit by a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And the voices that we heard have been again people who have been around you while you were taking the video; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These are children. I can hear children's voices. This is all in my hamlet. There were some other people taking videos as well. I don't know those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Judge Eser's questions and the answers by the witness were made and given while we were still at 47.564. We can proceed now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a question for Mr. Okanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, in the still shot we are looking at on the video you said it appears this the plane was dropping something and we could see something on the video. Do you recall what that was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably some sort of bomb. They wouldn't be dropping cakes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall, once -- if you saw an explosion on the ground immediately after?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely but if you play back the tape, sometimes there would be an explosion right afterwards and sometimes not. Maybe something went wrong with the bombs. It wasn't always the case that there was an explosion immediately afterwards, and some of them fell into the River Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that this is another plane. Were both of the planes that you observed that day dropping what appeared to be bombs? Or was it just one?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably both, but I can't remember now. Probably both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question with respect to the planes, when the planes arrived, did they immediately start dropping bombs or did this occur a little while after?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you about these details, I can see it better on the videotape now. I can't recall now because a lot of time has elapsed and I have forgotten. When I see the video, it jogs my memory but as for the details, I can't remember them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Ms. Richardson's questions were put and answered by the witness while we were still at 47.564.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you can see now is explosions in the woods above Sikiric. It means that it dropped bombs into the forest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement was made by the witness at 48.193.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my comment. I recognise my own voice. I'm saying that he was targeting something in the forest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this statement is made by the witness at 48.559.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you can see quite clearly that it's a different type of plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness makes this statement at 49.073.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are all voices you can hear from around me, and what you can see is the hamlet of Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness makes this statement at 50.376.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's us commenting and saying that they are all mixed up, you don't know who is where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness makes this statement at 51.504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there more?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that completes the ends of the video at 5318.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record could -- we just wanted to note now that we consider the transcript is incomplete, that there are things marked as inaudible which are actually audible. It's a matter we'll deal with in cross-examination and there some other things which are wrong as well, which we'll deal with subsequently, but just to mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said before it's a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We anticipate that there were things not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Ms. Richardson, we will have the break not at 10.30 as usual but at 10.45. So you've got another 20, 24, 22, 25, up to 25 minutes maximum.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Very good, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I just wanted to remind everyone there will be two sessions today with one break in between. And the sessions will be one hour and 45 minutes' length rather than one hour 30 minutes. I mean, it's -- and we'll finish at 1.00, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I do believe we need a P number for our transcript that we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you sure you do not have one transcript like this already handed in? I am under the impression that we had seen this before. Maybe I -- I saw it on the screen as well but --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm advised that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. This will be P ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 536, thank you. P536.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, why don't we give it P316.1? I think it will be better. Does it create a problem for you, Mr. Registrar? Just make sure that we don't have a P316 point something already. That's all. So this will be P316.1. And I'm repeating it because on line 14, page 28, although I had said it already, it did not show up in the transcript. Yes, let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, I'd like to ask you a few yes, sir about the comments that were made by yourself and others on the videotape. Well, first of all, I'd like to ask you if you recall how long the conflict that you were observing lasted in Bjelovac? The fighting.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: The whole day. I don't recall precisely, but I'm sure it was the whole day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a comment on the tape about -- I believe you said "What is happening to our men?" Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what you meant by that comment, as you were observing the fighting in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've explained when I was saying ours, our side, I was referring to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to see any of Bosnian Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was another comment made, I believe by someone standing and you explained that they were all mixed up as you were watching the fighting. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: That was a comment about what was happening to our men. We were saying that without knowing who was where or seeing anyone, we simply knew what the situation out there was and we were commenting on it. But I'm sure that the person standing next to me couldn't see anybody either at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later learn, if in fact there were Bosnian Serb soldiers during the attack on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were only villagers. They probably had lines that they held. I assume there was a demarcation line. But there was no need to keep troops there because it was only some ten, 15 or 20 houses. I can't be precise about the number, that were inhabited. I don't believe that there were soldiers in the village itself, although I don't know for sure. My answer is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned -- testified that there was conversation that could be heard on the tape, that was audible because of the radio communication or a radio that you had. Could you tell us the voices that you heard, were those Serbs or Muslims talking on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who, but my assumption is it was Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you base that assumption on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: In those actions, they used the radio much more than the Muslim side did. That's one thing. And although you can tell a little bit by the accent, that was not the rule. We who lived close by could guess more or less who was who by their accent, but this was not the rule. You couldn't be sure by the accent. I assumed that these were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that you believe that you could have been hit by a bullet. Could you just explain for us exactly where did you believe that bullet would have come from? Was it from the area in Bosnia where there was the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's when I was on the Drina. There was combat going on, and there could have been a stray bullet from the Bosnian side, and I could have been hit without being fired at deliberately. Although, at the time, I didn't see anyone near the Drina. I tried to look closely. I tried to spot someone but there was no one around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any firing coming from your village on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think later on there was some sort of a combat vehicle in the afternoon, but they must have crossed the Drina River from their side because our troops just weren't there. How do I know that? Later on, at some point, we asked our local police to set up a guard to protect us from attacks. We didn't have a proper army and we had no weapons. We might as well have ended up being the victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you feel it necessary to set up a village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: We knew there was very little food to go around, and it was unlikely that someone would come and try to kill us just because they hated us. It would more likely have been for the food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say someone, you mean from the Bosnian side and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one correction of the transcript. The transcript has not reflected the witness's words for some lines now and if we can have clarification from the witness, the witness said he knew the Muslims didn't have food and the transcript says there was no food around the place, and it's not quite the same as the witness says so if we can have clarification on that point, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, do you agree with what has just been said by Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, yes, Ms. Richardson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid that there would be looting of your village by individuals from across the river, the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's an inappropriately leading question. My learned friend could simply ask what fears, if any, did you have. There was a suggestion there that looting had indeed been taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection, sustained. Could you rephrase your question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think he's already answered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, he did. This is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We might as well move forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you set up the village guard, Mr. Okanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Once our official authorities failed to do anything about it, we self-organised, in a manner of speaking, and each hamlet had its own internal arrangement not to go out at night, and if someone needed to visit someone else at night, they were supposed to make their presence known and not to leave without announcing their departure so that we knew exactly who was moving about and who was knocking at our door. There was no public lighting to begin with so dark meant literally dark. It meant pitch black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may elaborate, even this village guard -- we stopped that once we realised that there was no danger, because nothing happened. After 10 days, we realised that nothing much had been happening and once the local authorities had ordered us to dig the trenches along the Drina for them to stand guard, we refused and they refused to provide security. But eventually there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- was the village guard set up after the attack on Bjelovac after the 14th of December?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that this is clear, the vehicle that you said that appeared on the 14th, that appeared on your side, on the Serbian side, could you tell us if that vehicle was firing across the river into the Bjelovac area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That vehicle was firing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it was quite far away so I couldn't tell the make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this JNA, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. It was too far to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, so that we are clear, and this was on the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time of the day did they appear, did that vehicle appear?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the vehicle around 1500 hours or between 15 and 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fighting had been going on for some time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: The fighting had been drawing to a close by that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was responsible for the attack on Bjelovac, the hamlet -- and the hamlet of Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Who, if anyone. I don't know, it's -- perhaps the question isn't objectionable but there isn't much foundation laid for how this witness would have any knowledge at all about it and it does suggest that maybe one person or one unit is responsible for what's being characterised as an attack, which the witness also didn't adopt the word attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, the use of the word attack, I agree 100 per cent with you. What worries me about the rest is that the witness has already told us that he never managed to see a single individual across the river. So -- his question was that whoever it was over there, they must have been pretty well concealed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later learn who, if anyone, whom was responsible for the burning of the houses on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no way I can know that. There is no way I can commit myself. The assumption is the Muslim forces, because Serbs lived in the area at the time. As to who it was, and who was involved in the fighting, the assumption is that the fighting was between Serbs and Muslims but once again I must say I simply didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I'd like to have a map shown to the witness. If I could have the assistance of the usher, we do have copies. The larger map is for the witness and copies, smaller copies, for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You gave me one extra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, if you could take a look at this map and locate your village and also locate the village of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, you have to put it further up. We need to see that -- we need to see that curve that there is on the map. It's further up. I mean the opposite. Yeah, that's it. And if we could centre that loop around that loop, and zoom in that area, please? Yup. No, we are going to lose it now. All right. Okay. That's perfect. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, if you could take a pen and circle --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I made a mistake here. Grabovica is right here and I'm well into Bosnia. This is Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness points at the name Grabovica on the map which is at ten o' clock or between ten and eleven o' clock of the loop where -- with the words "Drina." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can have the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can encircle that spot, the name, and put his initials against it. Just put the name of your village in a circle, please. All right. Okay. Can you please put your initials against that small circle that you have -- yes, that's Grabovica, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the -- for the record the witness also encircles, apart from Grabovica, he encircles Vhrpolje, which is between nine and ten o' clock with respect to the same loop mentioned earlier. Just put your initials against those two circles, please, if you can call them a circle. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour, if we could have the witness circle Bjelovac, which is directly across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think we can see them now. We don't need to ask the witness to point them out to us. Once he has pointed where he was, we can see what he could see across.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, if you could just show us -- point to what area the plane was flying over? You don't have to mark it, if you could just point to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Which plane, because there were several planes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because there were more than one, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The planes which were flying over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one, if you can remember, of course. The first plane, where did it -- where did it first appear from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They all came from this direction, from Bratunac. Some of them may have turned around at one point but they came back and they all came from this direction. They circled around here and then they would fly straight back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So for the record, the witness, while explaining, while making his statement, is pointing on the map to Bratunac and then drawing a line towards the loop mentioned earlier, where on the Serbian side there are Grabovica and Vhrpolje, and on the Bosnian side there is Sikirici and Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could I just add, Your Honour, and if the witness agrees that the witness also traced a line going over the road from Bratunac as being the route of the planes, as I saw it in any event, and perhaps he can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You've heard Mr. Jones. Would you agree to that, Mr. Okanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Jones. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the time and it appears --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we need -- yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic before we leave the map, you told us you had been down from your house to the Drina River. Could you indicate the spot from where you took the video when you have been went -- went, had been down to the river? Could you spot it on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was videoing right here from this small circle, and if you want the exact angle, I'll draw a line for you. It was in the direction of Sikiric so it was not at a right angle to the river because you have Bjelovac at a right angle and this is the centre of Bjelovac. If you draw a straight line from my house this would be the centre. It was obvious that the fighting was going on in Sikiric, the hamlet of Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has drawn two lines, starting from the circle he had put earlier on near Grabovica. One in the direction of Bjelovac and the other in the direction of Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But Mr. Okanovic you have not completely answered my question. I wanted to know which way you took from your house to the Drina River and from which point on the Drina River you took the video. Was it opposite Bjelovac or was it opposite Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between the two. I'll try to mark the spot roughly for you where I was on the Drina. It might have been around here. The houses you can see in the footage, the ones burning, they are over here. Do you want me to draw a circle? It might be around these parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has drawn a circle around an area which is at 11.00 above Sikirici. I think we can stop here for the time being. We will reconvene at quarter past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, you testified -- you testified that earlier that there were approximately 15 houses. I'd just like to clarify -- in Bjelovac, and I'd just like to clarify with you, were you talking about the entire Bjelovac area or just Sikiric, the hamlet itself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the number of houses. I don't know the exact number. It may be 18. It may be 10. It may as well be 30. You shouldn't take my word for it because I really don't know the exact number of houses and the clash that occurred obviously took place in Sikiric. It certainly wasn't Bjelovac. At least there was nothing being burned in Bjelovac. Were there any clashes in Bjelovac further down, I simply don't know. There were sounds of shooting coming from that general direction but you couldn't specify where from exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to see if there were individuals trying to cross the river from the Bosnian side into the Serbian -- into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: When I was on the Drina, there was a boat carrying someone from Bosnia, ferrying them to the other side. There was a wounded person there, middle aged. They ferried this man across the river and took him to the hospital and that's all I saw. The boat and then later on the boat went further down the Drina. It wasn't doing any serious transport work and it didn't go back to Bosnia. I just saw it leave down the Drina but I didn't take any footage because that was at night and there was this wounded man who needed to be ferried across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's give this map that we have been using before the break a number, please. It will be 536, correct? P536. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Grabovica, is there -- you mentioned -- you testified that you -- from where you were, you were unable to see individuals necessarily on the other side in Sikiric. Is there any point, location in Grabovica that it's -- you have a better vision of the other side, looking into Bjelovac-Sikiric area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: You could have a much better vision from the surrounding hills, especially if you had a pair of binoculars to use. With the naked eye, though, it would have been quite a distance, a kilometre and a half perhaps. It was very difficult to spot individual persons. Secondly, there were clashes taking place and people had to hide and conceal themselves but if I had seen any people, somebody else would have seen them too but it strikes me as logical that there was no one to be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the -- on the tape, the videotape, we could hear and you yourself stated that there were people commenting on people that -- at least that it was apparent from their comments that they could see people on the other side although you weren't able to see them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I object. That's a mischaracterisation of the evidence given. The witness said people next to him claimed to be essentially seeing people but he didn't think they were actually were able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Objection sustained. That is precisely what the witness stated earlier on. At one moment he even said "I can't understand how they could see anything themselves either."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that you had a radio with you on the day that you were filming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I have heard the witness say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I can put the question another way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- and perhaps it will become clearer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The voices that you said was coming over a radio, could you tell us exactly where this radio was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: The radio was tucked into my belt. It was a hand-held transportable radio station. The thing usually referred to as a walkie-talkie.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour at this time I'd like to have the witness be shown a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I see the photograph before it's shown to the witness, please? Yes. I wouldn't like or, rather, I don't want you to show the photograph to the witness before you actually ask him what kind of a radio it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I can put the preliminary questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you show him the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I can put the preliminary questions to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the radio you had, what kind of radio was it, and do you recall the make of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the make. It was a Jessie [phoen] walkie-talkie, I think, of Japanese make. It's 144/146 megahertz. It's used by ham radio operators, but that was the range. So we were able to listen to the police and they were using a higher frequency. It was a hand-held transportable radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd like the photograph shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, if you could take a look at the photograph that's before you, and tell the Trial Chamber whether this radio is similar to the one that you had with you on the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a Motorola. But it's more or less the same thing. It had a key board and it looked like this. This is probably a 5-watt device. I'm not sure about the range. It can have different ranges. It can have 144 or 130. I'm not sure which type this one is. But it's very much like this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to have this tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Noting, of course, the difference that the witness indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So this will be P537 [Realtime transcript read in error "P357"].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to just look at the photograph one more time when it's finished being marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the range of the radio you had, could you tell us whether or not you made any adjustments to the radio you had which enabled you to get better frequency or range?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a device whose range depends very much on the lie of the land, and this applies to every kind of device. If the conditions are good, if the area is not hilly, the range would be up to five kilometres. If you use this device from a hilltop, the range can be increased. If you use an elevated position. But if you have an external aerial. If you take this aerial off and use an external one, then you can dramatically increase the range both for reception and for emission. And then you can use it as a fixed radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to make these changes to your own radio?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I can remove the photograph. With respect to this -- the radio that you just described, could you tell the Trial Chamber what you used this radio for? What were you able to do with this radio?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I could use it to communicate with persons who were in possession of this same sort of device or a similar device and who were within the range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were in fact using this radio prior to the events on December 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's important why I obtained the radio in the first place. Do you want me to explain that, to give you the reason why I had it before the clash started?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that would be helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question would be when did you first obtain this radio and why, if you could just tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I obtained not one but three radios. I wanted to create a long-distance telephone. I don't know whether I can explain to anyone exactly how this works. Before the conflict, I did not have a telephone in that village. I used a telephone that was in Ljubovija and through a telephone mediator, I made a receiver and a hand-held radio station which I had, and I used this as a long distance telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start using the radio -- this radio itself, the radio that you just testified about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you with any precision. I really don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it during --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: But maybe two or three years at least before the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could think back to when the conflict arose in and around Srebrenica, did you have the radio then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you using it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you using it for?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I already had a telephone at home by that time. I used to send it as a telephone so I could send a signal from Ljubovija to Grabovica. That was about three or four kilometres away as the crow flies. But then I used it as a kind of phone because we didn't have mobile phones at that time. When the conflict broke out, then, of course, I joined in the communications. I communicated with those people because the telephone lines had been cut. Their telephones weren't working. And many of those people there, both Serbs and Muslims, came to us for assistance. They wanted to find out where someone was, whether they were all right. Someone would contact us from Bosnia on the radio station. They would give us a telephone number and say, please call this person and tell them that I'm fine. And there was no rule -- there were both Serbs and Muslims. We carried out this service for everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often did you engage in this service? Was it on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there every day. At that time, I was working on a cigarette factory in Podgorica, installing it. I was working in Centar and Coka [phoen] so I wasn't there every day. But when I was there I assisted as much as I could, but I can't really tell you precisely how much time I spent doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to being contacted for the purpose of communicating with family members and assisting in that manner, were you able to listen to conversations as well? Could you tell the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the Trial Chamber did. He said "yes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber which -- who you were able to listen to -- could you tell what you were listening -- who the individuals that were speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: How to explain this. It was working channel, as they call it, a frequency left open for communication among all, and there were both Serbs and Muslims using it. And the communications were quite correct, at least as far as I listened in. The communications were about who was where, there was even a lot of music. And I'm sure that special conversations were carried out on other frequencies. These were usual conversations, normal conversations. Someone might lose patience. For example, on one occasion, I heard that those were Serbs, I heard the person asking that someone should relieve him from his guard duty. Otherwise they would both abandon the place. And he even mentioned the name of the place, even though everybody was listening. He might as well have invited someone to come over and kill him. So you can see what kind of army this was, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell where the conversation was taking place? Was this in Serbia or in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly in Bosnia. I assume, at least, because I couldn't know from where the conversation was coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that individuals -- you would hear these conversations. Please tell us, did you hear Serbs talking to each other and Muslims talking to each other at some point?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Serbs were Serbs. Muslims with Muslims. And Serbs with Muslims, Muslims with Serbs. All those combinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain how it is you're able to distinguish between the voices of a Serb -- a person of Serb ethnicity and a person of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: With great difficulty, but if someone wants to declare themselves on the radio as a Muslim, well, you can tell by the sounds "č" and "ć." They are slightly softer. But as a rule, they could disguise their accents and then of course I wouldn't be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the conversation you just described about a duty station, well, first of all, could you tell us, with respect to that particular conversation you recall, was this individual who spoke on the radio of Serb ethnicity or Muslim ethnicity. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that was Serbian. I don't remember but I'm sure it was Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you heard conversations between Muslims, could you give us an example, if you recall, of the types of conversations that you would hear?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: When they joined in, and used this working channel as we called it, they talked among themselves, where are you, how are you doing? And you couldn't really glean any information from those conversations about who was doing what. They were just normal conversations, the usual kind of conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you overheard conversations between Serb and Muslim, was -- could you tell us, just in general, what types of conversations that you overheard?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: The usual kind of conversations. In spite of the fact that they were at war, when they communicated through the radio station, both sides were very correct. It was a kind of unwritten rule.
