If a Muslim was incorrect, his own Muslims would remove him from the radio, and the same applied to the Serbs, because if somebody had a very strong radio station, they could block the communication. They could exclude all the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can explain a little bit further, in more detail. When you say his own Muslims would remove him from the radio, could you explain to us how that would occur?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody knew -- first of all, the number of participants was not huge. It was a limited number. I can't tell you the exact number, but they were all more or less known, the names that joined in. And of course the Serbs knew who their own people were, and who was interfering with the communication, and the Muslims knew the same about the people on their side. They would know who was behaving improperly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said -- when you testified that the -- they would remove the conversation. Could you just explain in what way that would be done? Would the conversation be cut off? Just so that we have a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He could be a nuisance on that day but the next day they would know who he was and they would possibly take away his radio station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did individuals use their own names or were their code names used?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Usually it was code names or nicknames or made-up names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the range of the radio, your radio, and what you could overhear, could you tell the Trial Chamber upon what your ability to hear was based on? In other words was it just based on frequency? Did it matter what type of radio the other individuals had? Did everyone have to have the same type of radio?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has answered that question all right. He said the same or similar, plus within range.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would also depends on the configuration of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly and he's explained this already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what areas you were able to -- the range of your radio, what areas in the Bosnian area you were able to hear?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly those across the River Drina from where I was, Bjelovac, as far as Bratunac, because that was open, and the hills overlooking Srebrenica. If someone was talking on the radio in Srebrenica, for example, and not using a relay, then I would not be able to hear them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that individuals used code names. Did you yourself have a code name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you use the radio to communicate with other individuals outside of the need to assist with contacting family members?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. Did you speak with the Muslims and the Serb individuals that you would overhear?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often would you engage in discussions with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Not very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of conversations would you have with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, I would ask about someone I knew because I used to live in Bratunac. I had friends there among the Muslims as well. So I sometimes asked about them, and I communicated the most after the fall of Bjelovac, when the Muslims took Bjelovac. A woman went missing or rather two women went missing with two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you tell the Trial Chamber when it was that you were contacted, if in fact you were contacted, by someone looking for a woman and two children?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: That woman's husband, his mother was missing, his wife was missing, and his two children were missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I used to know it. I used to know it. Now I've forgotten. It escapes me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: The woman's name was Nada. That was his wife. I remember -- come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you recall it at some point, please let us know. How was it that -- why was it, I should say, that he came to you for assistance?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: He knew I had a radio station. I didn't know him personally before that time. But I did know the brothers of his wife. They were people who installed tiles. They tiled my house. And they told him about me, and said that I could communicate with both the Serb and the Muslim sides across the river, and nobody knew what had happened to this woman. First, people said that she jumped into the Drina and that she drowned, together with her children. Then we waited. I don't know whether I should use the name Naser or Gazda, but we were waiting for Naser to confirm whether he had taken that woman prisoner because if he could confirm that, then everything would be all right. She would be exchanged and we were sure they wouldn't hurt the woman with children. Also, there was fighting, and later on, I learned another piece of information from him, that this lady who had been taken prisoner had gone to school with Mr. Naser. She was a former schoolmate of his and that was another plus. But what mattered was that she was in his hands. There was a conflict. You know how it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe she was already -- I don't know, maybe she might have been killed in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you, Mr. Okanovic, for one moment. I think we need to go back a bit. When this individual came to you asking for assistance, could you tell the Trial Chamber what you did and who was it that you decided that you were going to contact to assist?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't really assist. You could just wait by the radio for Mr. Naser to make contact. We tried to call him through the radio station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you do that? Tell us the exact language you used in terms of contacting him. Did you -- how did you do it? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: The assumption was -- I don't know exactly, but that Mr. Naser used the name Gazda on the radio. I cannot confirm this because I didn't meet him personally, either before or after these events, but from what other people said and from the way he spoke, we assumed that this was Mr. Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back a bit prior to the individual coming to you to ask you to help him with finding -- finding out what happened to his wife and children. Did there come a time that you spoke with this person, Gazda?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Whether I spoke to him before or after, I can't tell you, but I did listen in. It's possible that I had spoken to him before. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm sure I did hear him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell the Trial Chamber what it was that you heard with respect to this individual, Gazda, prior to December 14. What were you able to hear on the radio with respect to this individual? In other words, did you hear people trying to contact him using this name or did you overhear conversations? Did you hear this person identify them self as such during the conversations you overheard?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He always introduced himself as Gazda. Later on, he didn't even have to introduce himself because we recognised his voice and I knew who he was, and so did others. After a time you learned to recognise voices. So that some people would say to him, you are Naser, you are Naser Oric. We know, but I really cannot confirm this. I can only say that this person introduced himself as Gazda and that we asked him for information about this missing person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person that you referred to as Gazda was it always the same voice responding in connection with this name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time prior to December 14th, as you listened to the radio, were other individuals trying to contact him as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When someone attempted to contact him, how would you know they were trying to reach him? Could you give us just an example of what you would hear as they are trying to contact him, reach out to him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: For example, "Gazda, it's Biber calling."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would he -- would this Gazda respond immediately?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was rarely on that frequency. I don't know when he was there. Maybe he would hear, but failed to respond. It didn't happen often that he responded. You can't say that he was there every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. How many channels did your radio have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could change channels. I can't tell you exactly how many, but also when I -- well, the radio was made for 144 to 146 megahertz. That's the amateur range. But you could reset it and increase the range. The quality of reception and the transmission in the extended range wasn't very good but it could still be done so that the number of channels might have been 50. I don't know. There were ten on the button itself but you could set as many as you liked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to December 14th, as you were just describing overhearing this conversation involving Gazda, could you tell us how many -- the period of time you heard this Gazda on the radio, whether he was talking or someone trying to reach out to him? Was it November, October, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the time when -- it's a very long time since then. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you use the radio every day?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I tell you I wasn't there every day. When I was there, then I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did say that. How often would you go away and how long did you stay away?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: A week at a time, or 10 days at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Getting back to the period of time when this individual came to you asking for assistance to locate his wife, what is it exactly you did with respect to contacting Gazda, who you believed to be Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I told him to sit next to the radio, wait and listen. I don't remember really how it went, whether I tried to call on him, but I don't believe, because there was fighting going on at the time, I don't believe he would have been listening to that channel which was used for general communication. On the second or third day, I went to Italy and stayed there three or four days. I wasn't there at all. This man was by the radio station, but I think that Gazda responded and said that the woman was in his keeping, that she was safe, and that there would be no problems. And this was about five or six days later. When I got back, whether they learned this before, I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were listening to the radio, did Gazda, this person you call Gazda, respond and said something directly to you? Or did you talk directly to him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the occasion was, whether it was on that occasion, but I think it was, when we learned that the woman was there, I told him that it wasn't right for him to imprison women and children. I told him this was a war crime. And he responded that it wasn't that. He had saved them and kept them safe. What the verbal communication was, I really can't recall now, but that was gist of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time this conversation took place, was the woman's husband with you? Was he also listening?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure he was. He never left the radio except when he went to sleep. He was at my house all day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Gazda, was this the same voice associated with the name that you had heard prior to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this person come, this Gazda, the voice that you heard, on the radio, did -- was he specifically seeking you, responding to your calling him, or was he talking to someone else and you injected?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now. I can't remember what exactly happened, how the situation evolved. But later both the communication and the exchange were arranged elsewhere and I had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he -- do you recall if he said anything to you with respect to yourself and your ability to listen in on conversations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion he told me he knew who I was. He didn't say my name because it wasn't customary for us to use names, even if we knew who was on the other end of the line. He said you're the electrical engineer from Vhrpolje who is able to catch all the frequencies. And I told him, "Well, I'm not quite the man, but still, he can send greetings to a schoolmate I have over there."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could I mention one quick matter before it disappears off our screen. It's in the transcript, and it may be a small thing but I think it has to be crystal clear. It's on line 19 on page 54. It's "And he responded that it wasn't that he had saved them and kept them safe," as if it were one sentence. As I clearly heard it, and I think we all did, is it's -- he responded that "It wasn't that." Full stop. "He had saved them and kept them safe."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to make absolutely sure that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is another correction to the transcript correction while we're on this topic. It's with respect to the Exhibit number, the photograph, it -- I believe it's P537 and I think the transcript reflects P357 and that's at line 42, 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Gazdas were there at the time that were you listening on the radio, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had asked the question and he had answered it already, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when this individual, Gazda, came on the frequency, were people -- was he treated any differently from any of the other individuals communicating via the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what exactly you mean by "differently". He was obviously a rather important person because there were many people who asked to speak to him. He was often called upon, sometimes he responded and sometimes he didn't, but whenever he did he would usually talked to several people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the conversation that you had with him about the women and children last? I believe I see Defence standing up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let him answer the question first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one correction for the transcript and the witness can clarify that. The witness said that he was often called and that he didn't often respond, whereas the transcript says sometimes he responded and sometimes he didn't, which is quite different. So if that can be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you said, Witness, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes he responded and sometimes he didn't. We don't know if he was listening. There is no way you can know whether there is someone on the other end listening when you're calling so the question was maybe he would respond, or maybe he would respond if he was there at the time and if he was listening. We had no confirmation there was any presence at all on the other end of the line refusing to respond. Therefore, I'm not sure what you mean. Anyone who is familiar with radio communication clearly realises that this is not a legitimate question. We don't know whether the person perhaps didn't wish to respond. We didn't know if the person was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Stop there. Ms. Richardson, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm almost finished my examination. Could I have a moment? It appears Your Honour the transcript what the witness has responded to Madam Vidovic's question is it doesn't reflect that it's the witness. It actually has on the transcript that it's Madam Vidovic so perhaps we could make a correction there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ah, yes, that's a very important matter that you have raised. We are talking of line 7 on page 57. It says "Ms. Vidovic, interpretation, what you said, Witness, please if you can." And then there is "werp, werp." Where there is "werp, werp," that's where the witness starts so it should be on a fresh line. And what that "werp, werp," I don't know what it means but certainly that's where the witness starts responding to Ms. Vidovic's question. Just for the record. And then it ends at line 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, did there come a time after the conversation you had with Gazda that you spoke to him again or that you heard him on the radio again?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps three or four times, but every time it was informal. Three or four times that I talked, but I heard him more often than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever following December of 1992 -- did you meet with individual -- the woman that you mentioned, her husband had come to you about and to assist?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She came to see me two or three times. But it was right after the liberation, but later I never saw her again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she confirm to you that she had in fact been held?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: She confirmed that she had been not in a prison but in a private home. She said she was treated in a fair manner and that both she and the children were fed properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jones, I know that I had told you, you will start on Monday but little did I know that Ms. Richardson for once would finish before the time. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I approach it this way, Your Honour? We would like to cross-examine this witness in a sequence which would start with the videotapes and we do actually need time to consider the testimony which has been given, fairly technical matters, of the -- where various evidence was given in relation to the video. And our understanding, of course, would be that we would start on Monday and we would prefer to start with that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is, however, one question I would ask simply because it will help with the planning, it may help to save time on Monday which, if I could therefore start my cross-examination with one question and then continue and finish on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Go ahead. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, it's simply there. The video which we saw today, we saw there was a date, and times in the frames. It's right, isn't it, that that was accurate, as far as you know, the times which appear on the screen? You had calibrated the video beforehand? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. It was simply that. So if we could continue on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. So Mr. Okanovic we give you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll give you a rest now. We will reconvene on Monday. Monday we are sitting in the morning. That's the only day in the week that we are sitting in the morning, actually, and I don't know if it's in this same courtroom or not. I think it is in the same courtroom. And we will continue and finish with your testimony on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
